case_study_insert.main_stem: Havenport Seafood Producers (HSP) is a public limited company in the seafood-processing sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1985 by Nadia Havenport, it supplies frozen seafood to national supermarket chains and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. HSP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new freezing and processing plant, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 from a share issue. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $13.50, and currently produces 120,000 units a year for its customers. HSP faces two problems: quality complaints of 34 a month and a defect rate of 3.8%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The plant processed 30,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.8%, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 34 a month. Average order fulfilment is 2.5 days. A survey of 900 shoppers found that 66% would pay up to $0.45 more for sustainably sourced seafood and 63% check sustainability labels. Training records show 26 of 120 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new freezing line; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $1,050 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Havenport Seafood Producers as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.6% to 5.35%, increasing the cost of variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.5% from $13.40 to $14.27 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills. (3) Fish and energy input costs have risen 13.1% year-on-year, food-price inflation is 8.0% and consumer spending on frozen seafood grew 2.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HSP plans to fund part of its freezing-plant expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for HSP of using a share issue instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $500,000 share issue brings equity that does not have to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, so HSP avoids adding debt service to fixed costs of $480,000 a year alongside the $700,000 bank loan. Cash is preserved for tackling the 3.8% defect rate and the 34 monthly complaints, protecting the $6.00 contribution on each of 120,000 units. Unlike a loan, no assets need be offered as security for the new freezing plant.

Point 2: Equity improves the company's debt capacity for future borrowing, since the new shares increase capital employed without raising liabilities. As a public limited company, HSP can access shareholders through the market, and founder Nadia Havenport can retain control if the new shares are placed with supportive investors. With democratic leadership in a hierarchical structure, the extra capital lets decision-makers invest in quality improvements without a bank imposing repayment conditions, whereas heavy borrowing would strain the $1,200,000 project if the 3.8% defects persisted.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HSP's $500,000 shares, $700,000 loan, defects and output.

questions.question_text: HSP is launching its new sustainably sourced seafood range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should HSP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A TV campaign would reach millions and build rapid awareness of sustainable seafood across all the supermarket chains stocking HSP. The cost is high, however, and a large share of viewers will not buy frozen seafood or fall outside the distribution network, so spending is inefficient. For a 120-employee plc with $480,000 fixed costs and a $700,000 loan, the budget could be better directed at quality, especially with 34 complaints a month, than at mass airtime.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is inexpensive and suits a localised message, reaching listeners near the processing plant. Its reach is too narrow for national supermarket distribution: HSP must sell 120,000 units a year, so local audiences cannot generate the necessary volume, and radio cannot illustrate the sustainability story that the research highlights.

Social media influencer marketing: Influencers can demonstrate sourcing practices to the 66% of 900 surveyed shoppers who would pay $0.45 more and the 63% checking sustainability labels, with precise targeting, national coverage and measurable engagement. Results develop more slowly than TV and depend on credibility, but the fit with survey evidence is strongest and cost per reached shopper is low.

Recommendation: HSP should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the identified shoppers nationally, is cheaper than television and supports the premium needed for a $6.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as wasteful and costly; radio is rejected because it cannot deliver the national reach required by supermarket contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited HSP context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in HSP's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: HSP receives 34 quality complaints a month and has a defect rate of 3.8%. Explain two benefits for HSP of using quality circles to involve employees in reducing defects.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles bring the 120 workers together in small groups to identify causes of the 3.8% defect rate on the freezing line, using the practical knowledge of operators who see faults first-hand. Their suggestions can cut defects below the current 3.8% and reduce the 34 monthly complaints, protecting the $13.50 selling price with national supermarkets and the $6.00 contribution on 120,000 units without major new capital spending beyond the $1,200,000 plant.

Point 2: Quality circles give staff a voice, which suits HSP's democratic leadership despite its hierarchical structure and can raise morale and commitment. Greater involvement may reduce the need to retrain the 26 of 120 employees still awaiting on-the-job training at $1,050 a head for college courses, and it can stabilise output while the new freezing plant is commissioned, helping meet the 30,000-unit quarterly throughput target.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of quality circles (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HSP's 3.8% defects, 34 complaints and training.

questions.question_text: HSP must upskill 26 staff to operate the new freezing line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should HSP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Instruction at the freezing line matches HSP's own equipment and quality standards, costs no fees and keeps the 26 trainees productive while learning, safeguarding the 30,000 units processed last quarter and progress in cutting defects from 5.1% to 3.8%. Its weaknesses are that trainers are production staff whose duties suffer, poor habits may be copied, and there is no certificate that supermarket auditors might require.

Off-the-job training: The college course costs $1,050 per employee, or $27,300 for 26 staff — manageable next to a $1,200,000 investment — and gives structured, up-to-date knowledge plus a recognised qualification. It removes 26 of 120 workers from the line temporarily, reducing capacity and possibly worsening the 34 monthly complaints during the transition, and generic content may not match HSP's exact freezing settings without on-site follow-up.

Decision: HSP should choose on-the-job training for the rollout and add short college modules for lead operators later. It is machine-specific, avoids $27,300 in fees and protects throughput while defects stand at 3.8%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 26 of 120 staff would slow the 30,000-unit quarterly pack and the generic course cannot teach plant-specific controls; certified modules can follow once the line is stable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited HSP context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in HSP's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in context with a justified decision on cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HSP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 80,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four applied uses: margin of safety of 40,000 units; average total cost of $11.50; labour productivity of 1,000 units per worker; servicing the $700,000 loan.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($13.50 − $7.50) = $480,000 ÷ $6.00 = 80,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 80,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.50 − $7.50 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HSP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 80,000 units against output of 120,000 units gives a margin of safety of 40,000 units, showing the buffer against 3.8% defects and 34 complaints.
2. Average total cost of $480,000 ÷ 120,000 + $7.50 = $11.50 a unit benchmarks the freezing process.
3. Labour productivity of 120,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 1,000 units per worker indicates whether staffing is efficient.
4. Contribution of $6.00 sets the volume needed to service the $700,000 bank loan used for the $1,200,000 plant.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HSP's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HSP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.97 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $160,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $425,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $195,000 + $82,000 = $462,000. Dividing by $300,000 and $285,000 current liabilities gives 1.42 and 1.62. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($425,000 − $210,000) ÷ $300,000 = 0.72; 2025 = ($462,000 − $185,000) ÷ $285,000 = 0.97.

Evaluation: Liquidity is stronger in both measures. The current ratio rose from 1.42 to 1.62 as current assets grew by $37,000 and current liabilities fell by $15,000, giving more cover for short-term obligations while HSP services a $700,000 loan. The acid test rising from 0.72 to 0.97 is the stronger evidence of genuine improvement because it excludes $210,000 of stock in 2024 and $185,000 in 2025, which for frozen seafood could be slow to realise if the 3.8% defect rate persists. Cash increased from $55,000 to $82,000, adding flexibility. The reservation is that trade receivables rose from $160,000 to $195,000 with supermarkets, tying up cash, and the acid test still remains below 1, so HSP is not yet able to cover all current debts without inventory.

Conclusion: HSP's liquidity has improved, since both ratios are higher and the progress is not dependent on building stock. However, receivables growth and an acid test of 0.97 mean the company should tighten credit control before further borrowing for the $1,200,000 plant.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios, evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities, and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HSP of promoting its seafood as sustainably sourced.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: In a survey of 900 shoppers, 66% would pay up to $0.45 more for sustainably sourced seafood and 63% check sustainability labels. That supports a premium over the $13.50 price and protects the $6.00 contribution per unit against 13.1% fish and energy inflation, while helping sell 120,000 units through national supermarkets and justifying the $1,200,000 freezing plant.

Disadvantage: Sustainable sourcing can raise the $7.50 variable cost per unit, and the insert provides no breakdown of that cost, so the exact impact cannot be quantified; if the $0.45 premium is not accepted on the whole range, margin will fall. There is also a reputational risk: if a sourcing claim is challenged by the 63% who check labels, demand could drop just as HSP faces 34 complaints a month and a 3.8% defect rate, while the $700,000 loan still needs cash.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using HSP's survey data, costs and quality record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.35%, the 6.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.1% rise in fish and energy input costs will affect HSP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.6% to 5.35%): On a variable-rate $700,000 ten-year loan the extra annual cost is 0.75% × $700,000 = $5,250 (0.0075 × $700,000), modest beside $480,000 fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed. Higher rates may also cool consumer spending on frozen seafood and make future finance dearer, but fixing the rate can mostly neutralise this.

Minimum wage increase (6.5%, to $14.27 an hour): The workforce of 120 means this feeds directly into the wage bill and cannot be refused. Because the insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, a valid annual wage total cannot be invented. The sound comparison is productivity: 120,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 1,000 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if that productivity is maintained or output grows; otherwise unit labour cost reduces the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (13.1% fish and energy): The $7.50 variable cost is not decomposed, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole $7.50 rose 13.1%, that adds $0.98 a unit (0.131 × $7.50), about $117,600 a year at 120,000 units. Even partial pass-through would materially reduce contribution, though the $0.45 sustainability premium and 2.6% demand growth recover some.

Conclusion: The 13.1% rise in fish and energy input costs will have the greatest impact: it applies to every unit and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution supporting the $1,200,000 investment. The interest effect is a known $5,250 and the wage effect depends on unstated hours, whereas input inflation is large, continuous and difficult to offset quickly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited HSP application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HSP's costs and finance in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes and concludes input-cost inflation has the greatest impact with reasons.
